Learning Objectives
Apply strategies for deep vein thrombosis/pulmonary embolism prophylaxis in orthopaedic
patients.
Discuss evaluation strategies for suspected deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism.
Review treatment principles for deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism.
Epidemiology
Rates of pulmonary embolism are unacceptably high in untreated patients. Treatment lowers
the risk of pulmonary embolism; therefore, all patients undergoing major orthopaedic surgery
should be considered for prophylactic treatment.


Epidemiology
Without prophylaxis, patients with a proximal femur fracture have a reported prevalence
of fatal pulmonary embolism as high as 7%. Historically, patients undergoing elective
total hip arthroplasty (THA) and total knee arthroplasty (TKA) have rates of symptomatic
pulmonary embolism as high as 20% and 8%, respectively, without prophylaxis.1,2 Rates
of symptomatic pulmonary embolism in the setting of modern thromboprophylaxis
protocols are estimated to be 0.37% for TKA and 0.21% for THA.3,4
Risk Factors for Venous Thromboembolism
(Table 1)
Risks should be assessed preoperatively. If necessary, patients may benefit from consultation
with hematology if a coagulation disorder is suspected.
Table 1 Risk Factors for Thromboembolic Disease
History of prior thromboembolic event
Advanced age
Obesity
Malignant disease
Genetic hypercoagulable state
Oral contraceptive use
Pregnancy

Major orthopaedic surgery
History of myocardial infarction/stroke/congestive heart failure


Risk Factors for Venous Thromboembolism
Risks may be cumulative; a combination of risk factors in a given patient may greatly
increase their risk for venous thromboembolism. Patients with a history of a
thromboembolic event deserve special attention given the numerous inherited
hypercoagulable states (such as factor V Leiden) that have been identified. Preoperative
consultation with a hematologist may be appropriate.1,5
Specific fracture types and patterns, including major pelvic and acetabular fractures and
multiple extremity injuries, are associated with an extremely high risk for deep vein
thrombosis (DVT)/pulmonary embolism. In these cases, a maximal prophylactic
approach must be taken, combining chemical and pneumatic options in all patients if
possible. In addition, fracture fixation can be performed in some patients without
withholding chemical prophylaxis without the risk of considerable bleeding.
Pathophysiology
DVT is the end result of a complex interaction of events, including activation of the clotting
cascade and platelet aggregation.
The Virchow triad (predisposing factors) is composed of three factors: venous stasis,
endothelial damage, and hypercoagulability.6
Venous stasis commonly occurs in orthopaedic patients secondary to immobility and non–
weight-bearing status. Without normal muscle contractions to achieve pressure gradients in
the venous system, stasis occurs. Intraoperative vascular congestion also may result from
extremity positioning, retractor placement, tourniquet use, and other mechanical factors.
Endothelial damage may occur secondary to traumatic injuries or surgical trauma. This may
lead to exposure of underlying collagen and von Willebrand factor, leading to adhesion of
circulating platelets. Underlying smooth muscle cells and currently activated surrounding
endothelial cells express tissue factor that binds the circulating coagulation factor VII.7
Hypercoagulability secondary to patient factors, or a hypercoagulable state induced by
surgical factors, can occur. A large release of thrombogenic factors may occur during
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:00 AM
AAOS | Venous Thromboembolic Disease
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000654
3/22

pressurization of the femoral canal, especially in cemented THA, leading to the release of
tissue factor, collagen fragments, fibrinogen, and tissue thromboplastin.
Prophylaxis
Given the high risk of venous thromboembolism (VTE) in patients undergoing major
orthopaedic surgery, the difficulty in diagnosing these events, and the morbidity and mortality
associated with these events (approximately two-thirds of patients who sustain a fatal
pulmonary embolism die within 60 minutes of the development of symptoms), some form of
prophylaxis is necessary.
The optimal duration of prophylaxis is unclear; however, patients may be at risk for VTE for
several weeks postoperatively.
American College of Chest Physicians (CHEST) guidelines for patients undergoing major
orthopaedic surgery (THA, TKA, and hip fracture surgery; Table 2)
American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons guidelines for patients undergoing TKA or THA8
Table 2 Highlights: Prevention of Venous Thromboembolism in Orthopaedic Surgery.
American College of Chest Physicians Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guidelines, ed 9
2.1.1
In patients undergoing THA or TKA, we recommend use of one of the following for
a minimum of 10 to 14 d rather than no antithrombotic prophylaxis: LMWH,
fondaparinux, apixaban, dabigatran, rivaroxaban, LDUH, adjusted-dose VKA,
aspirin (all grade 1B), or an IPCD (grade 1C)
2.2
For patients undergoing major orthopaedic surgery (THA, TKA, HFS) and receiving
LMWH as thromboprophylaxis, we recommend starting either 12 h or more
preoperatively or 12 h or more postoperatively rather than within 4 h or less
preoperatively or 4 h or less postoperatively (grade 1B)
2.3.1
In patients undergoing THA or TKA, irrespective of the concomitant use of an IPCD
or length of treatment, we suggest the use of LMWH in reference to the other
agents we have recommended as alternatives: fondaparinux, apixaban,
dabigatran, rivaroxaban, LDUH (all grade 2B), adjusted-dose VKA, or aspirin (all
grade 2C)
2.4
For patients undergoing major orthopaedic surgery, we suggest extending
thromboprophylaxis in the outpatient period for up to 35 d from the day of
surgery rather than for only 10 to 14 d (grade 2B)

4/22

2.5
In patients undergoing major orthopaedic surgery, we suggest using dual
prophylaxis with an antithrombotic agent and an IPCD during the hospital stay
(grade 2C)
2.6
In patients undergoing major orthopaedic surgery who have an increased risk of
bleeding, we suggest using an IPCD or no prophylaxis rather than pharmacologic
treatment (grade 2C)
2.8
In patients undergoing major orthopaedic surgery, we suggest against using filter
placement for primary prevention over no thromboprophylaxis in patients with an
increased bleeding risk or contraindications to pharmacologic and mechanical
thromboprophylaxis (grade 2C)
2.9
For asymptomatic patients after major orthopaedic surgery, we recommend
against Doppler (or duplex) ultrasonography screening before hospital discharge
(grade 1B)
HFS = hip fracture surgery, IPCD = intermittent pneumatic compression device, LDUH = low-
dose unfractionated heparin, LMWH = low-molecular-weight heparin, THA = total hip
arthroplasty, TKA = total knee arthroplasty, VKA = vitamin K antagonist.
Reproduced from Lieberman JR: Guest editorial: American College of Chest Physicians
evidence-based guidelines for venous thromboembolic prophylaxis. The guideline wars are
over. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2012;20(6):333-335.

Prophylaxis
The latest version of the CHEST clinical practice guidelines was published in 2012 and
currently are similar to the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons guidelines for
patients undergoing TKA or THA, with increased emphasis on agent safety. Currently,
low-dose aspirin is considered an acceptable form of prophylaxis; however, low-
molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) continues to be preferred for prophylaxis (this is a
weaker recommendation).9 Many of the changes were made because the committee
did not base its recommendations on venographic screening of asymptomatic
patients (which was used heavily in the past).10
No specific recommendation for any particular agent or dosing regimen for
prophylaxis exists because the current literature was not thought to support one
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:00 AM
AAOS | Venous Thromboembolic Disease
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000654
5/22

regimen over any other given the network meta-analysis that was used to examine
the literature. The following is a summary of specific recommendations.
Strong recommendation: recommend against routine postoperative duplex
ultrasonography screening
Moderate recommendation: suggest the use of pharmacologic and/or mechanical
compression devices in patients not at risk for VTE or bleeding beyond that of the
surgical procedure itself; no specific recommendation for any one agent exists
because the available evidence was thought to be inadequate to distinguish among
agents.
Weak recommendation: patients undergoing elective TKA and THA already have a
high risk for VTE; the practitioner might further assess the risk of VTE by determining
if patients have had a previous VTE event.
Consensus recommendation (absence of reliable evidence)—Assess patients
undergoing elective TKA or THA for known bleeding disorders and active liver
disease.
Physicians and patients should discuss the duration of prophylaxis. Patients
undergoing elective TKA or THA who have had previous VTE should receive
pharmacologic and mechanical prophylaxis.
Patients undergoing elective TKA or THA who have a known bleeding disorder or
active liver disease should receive mechanical prophylaxis only.
Patients undergoing elective TKA or THA should undergo early mobilization.
Inconclusive recommendations (current evidence unclear): no recommendation for
or against assessing for VTE risk factors other than a history of previous VTE for
elective TKA or THA.
Do not recommend for or against assessing for bleeding risk factors other than
known bleeding disorder or active liver disease for elective TKA or THA.
Do not recommend for or against specific prophylactic strategy in patients
undergoing elective TKA or THA and who do not have an elevated risk for VTE or
bleeding beyond that of the surgical procedure itself.
Do not recommend for or against inferior vena cava (IVC) filters in patients
undergoing elective TKA or THA who also have a contraindication to
chemoprophylaxis and/or known residual venous thromboembolic disease.11
The Orthopaedic Trauma Association also has issued recommendations for patients
with a fracture.12
SEND FEEDBACK

6/22

Chemical prophylaxis—30 mg of enoxaparin twice daily is the optimal form of VTE
prophylaxis; should be initiated within 24 hours in all patients with no
contraindications (rating: strong).
If LMWH is contraindicated, other agents can be used but are not recommended
instead of LMWH (rating: moderate).
Combined prophylaxis with LMWH and calf sequential compression devices is
recommended if possible (rating: strong)
Continuation of VTE prophylaxis in trauma patients for at least 1 month after
discharge (evidence: limited)
In patients with isolated lower extremity injuries and no other risk factors who
can independently mobilize, chemical prophylaxis is not recommended (rating:
moderate).
Screening—Screening for DVT is not recommended in asymptomatic trauma
patients (rating: strong).
IVC filters—The routine use of IVC filters in low and high-risk trauma patients to
prevent pulmonary embolism is not recommended unless the patient has a
documented pulmonary embolism or DVT despite appropriate prophylaxis (rating:
strong).
IVC placement may be considered in patients thought to be at high risk for VTE
with contraindications to acceptable anticoagulant agents (rating: moderate).
Mechanical approaches
Sequential compression devices
Act via increasing peak venous flow to decrease venous stasis
Stimulate the fibrinolytic system
Present no risk of bleeding
Poor patient compliance and/or inappropriate application are common.
Good efficacy has been shown in patients who undergo TKA.
Increased interest in the use of home mechanical compression exists,
especially with decreased hospital length of stays. Additional research on costs
and compliance are necessary13
Plantar compression devices
Compression of the venous plexus of the foot produces pulsatile flow in the
deep venous system of the leg (simulates walking).
Inadequate data are available to recommend these devices alone.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:00 AM
AAOS | Venous Thromboembolic Disease
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000654
7/22

Graduated compression stockings
These stockings produce a pressure differential between the distal and
proximal portions of the lower extremity, decreasing venous stasis.
These stockings should be a useful adjunct only and not the sole means of
prophylaxis.
Pharmacologic approaches (Table 3)
Unfractionated heparin (UFH)
Binds to antithrombin III, potentiating its inhibitory effect on thrombin (factor
IIa) and factor Xa
Higher risk of bleeding and lower efficacy than LMWH
Increased risk of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, which is secondary to
heparin-dependent antibodies that activate platelets
Fixed, low-dose heparin (5,000 U administered subcutaneously two or three
times daily) generally is not effective in orthopaedic patients.
Reversed via protamine sulfate
LMWH
LMWH is derived from the fractionation of UFH into smaller, more homogenous
molecules.
LMWH is unable to bind antithrombin III and thrombin simultaneously and,
therefore, has a greater inhibitory effect on factor Xa than factor IIa (thrombin).
Provides superior protection against DVT and does not inhibit hemostasis as
vigorously at surgical sites compared with UFH.
Less inhibition of platelet function and less vascular permeability than UFH.
Improved bioavailability (90% versus 35% for UFH)
Longer half-life (less frequent dosing)
Laboratory monitoring is not required.
First full dose 12 to 24 hours postoperatively or until hemostasis is achieved at
the surgical site
Should not be used in combination with an indwelling epidural catheter or in
patients in whom a traumatic neuraxial anesthetic has been administered
(secondary to a risk of epidural bleeding). Neuraxial anesthesia can be
performed 12 hours after the administration of LMWH.
Compared with warfarin, LMWH is associated with a decreased risk of
venographically identified DVT but a higher risk of bleeding complications.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:00 AM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000654
8/22

Excretion is primarily renal; therefore, dosing needs to be adjusted in patients
with chronic renal failure.
Several agents currently are available, and pharmacokinetics, dosing, and
outcomes differ among agents.14,15
More recent trend is weight-based therapy rather than standard daily or twice-
daily dosing in higher-risk patients.
Prophylactic dosing of enoxaparin may be 40 mg daily or 30 mg twice daily.
Renal dosing is suggested for patients with a creatinine clearance level less
than 30 mL/min
Fondaparinux
Synthetic pentasaccharide and an indirect factor Xa inhibitor
Decreased incidence of venographically identified DVT compared with
enoxaparin in patients with hip fracture and TKA
Trend toward an increased risk of bleeding complications
Not recommended in patients who weigh less than 50 kg or those with renal
insufficiency; has not been used in combination with indwelling epidural
catheters.16,17
Dosing is 2.5 mg/d subcutaneously; first dose can be administered 6 to 12
hours postoperatively.
Warfarin
Antagonizes vitamin K, which prevents the y-carboxylation of glutamic acid
required for the synthesis of factors II, VII, IX, and X and proteins C and S.
Typical dosing regimens begin on the night of surgery as soon as the patient
can tolerate oral pain medications.
The anticoagulant effect is delayed for 24 to 36 hours after the initiation of
therapy, and the target international normalized ratio often is not achieved
until 3 days postoperatively.
Warfarin interacts with many other medications that can augment its effect
(Table 4).
Not recommended for use in combination with NSAIDs secondary to a higher
risk of bleeding at the surgical and nonsurgical sites (particularly
gastrointestinal bleeding)
Patients who ingest large amounts of vitamin K–rich foods (eg, green, leafy
vegetables) may require increased doses to achieve the target international
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:00 AM
AAOS | Venous Thromboembolic Disease
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000654
9/22

normalized ratio.
Reversible with vitamin K administration; complete reversal can take several
days. Fresh-frozen plasma is administered if immediate reversal is required.
The target level of anticoagulation has been controversial; however, a target
international normalized ratio of 2.0 is appropriate for prophylactic use in
orthopaedic patients.
Aspirin
Aspirin irreversibly binds to and inactivates cyclooxygenase in developing and
circulating platelets, which blocks the production of thromboxane A2, the
necessary prostaglandin for platelet aggregation.
Currently, aspirin frequently is used as a prophylactic agent after total joint
arthroplasty and is approved in CHEST guidelines. Aspirin may be less potent
than other chemoprophylactic agents and may not be ideal in patients with
higher rates of pulmonary embolism (ie, history of pulmonary embolism or
DVT, slow to mobilize).
The Pulmonary Embolism Prevention Trial was a randomized, double-blind
study of aspirin versus placebo in 17,000 patients with a hip fracture or patients
undergoing elective TKA or THA.18 The study showed that aspirin reduced the
risk of fatal pulmonary embolism and symptomatic nonfatal DVT and
pulmonary embolism.
In a randomized controlled trial of 3,424 patients who underwent THA or TKA,
patients received rivaroxaban (10 mg/day) until postoperative day five and were
then randomized to continue rivaroxaban (10 mg/day) or receive aspirin (81 mg
twice/day). The duration of additional treatment was 9 days for patients who
underwent TKA and 30 days for patients who underwent THA. At 90 days
postoperatively, symptomatic DVT was not different between groups, with rates
less than 1%. No difference in bleeding complications were observed.19
If combined with neuraxial anesthetic agents and particularly hypotensive
epidural techniques, aspirin appears to be associated with a lower risk of
postoperative thromboembolic events secondary to enhanced blood flow in the
lower extremities.
Data exist to support prolonged prophylaxis (up to 35 days) in patients who
have undergone THA; however, prolonged prophylaxis has not been shown to
have an effect in patients who have undergone TKA.9

Dosing for aspirin is controversial, with various reports and regimens shown to
be effective. Dosing may be 325 mg once or twice daily. Reduced VTE also has
been reported with 81 mg twice daily.20
In a large multicenter, randomized noninferiority study of trauma patients who
underwent surgical treatment for a lower or upper extremity fracture and
patients with a pelvic or acetabular fractures, 12,211 total patients were
randomized to receive aspirin (81 mg twice/day) or LMWH (30 mg twice/day).
Aspirin was noninferior to LMWH in preventing death, death related to
pulmonary embolism, and nonfatal pulmonary embolism. Although the mean
rate of DVT was low in the aspirin group (2.51%), it was higher than that in the
LMWH group (1.71%). Bleeding events were similar between the groups.21
Rivaroxaban
Factor Xa inhibitor
Daily dosing beginning 12 to 24 hours postoperatively.
12 days for TKA, 35 days for THA
2.5 mg twice daily for prophylaxis
Reversal agent: andexanet alfa
Advantages: oral administration, fixed daily dosing, monitoring not required
Disadvantages: bleeding risks, reversal agent poorly defined, cost22
Apixaban
Factor Xa inhibitor
Twice daily dosing beginning 12 to 24 hours postoperatively; 12 days ± 3 days
for TKA and 35 days ± 3 days for THA
Prophylactic dosing of 2.5 mg twice daily
Reversal agent: andexanet alfa
Advantages: oral administration, fixed oral dosing (twice daily), monitoring not
required
Disadvantages: bleeding risks, reversal agent poorly defined, cost23
Dabigatran
Direct thrombin inhibitor
Oral administration
DVT/pulmonary embolism prophylaxis for THA only; begin on postoperative day
1: 220 mg daily for 28 to 35 days
Reversal agent: idarucizumab24

At the 2022 International Consensus Meeting on Venus Thromboembolism, 600
international experts issued a set of guidelines for orthopaedic patients.25
A history of VTE is a risk factor for postoperative VTE. Varicose veins and superficial
venous thrombosis also are risk factors for VTE in patients undergoing lower
extremity orthopaedic surgery.
Scoring systems for VTE risk stratification are not reliable because they generally
have not been validated in large patient populations.
The recommended duration of post-hospital VTE prophylaxis after TKA and THA is
14 to 35 days. Based on efficacy, safety, and costs, aspirin is the optimal
prophylactic agent.
Often, patients are administered multimodal analgesic agent, including NSAIDs.
The use of NSAIDs may reduce the antiplatelet effect of aspirin; therefore, if
combined, aspirin should be administered at 2 hours before NSAIDs.

Diagnosis

Diagnosis
The diagnosis of DVT and pulmonary embolism may be challenging in the immediate
postoperative setting if lower extremity swelling, pain, and pain on forced dorsiflexion of
the foot (Homan sign) are common. Tachycardia often is observed secondary to pain and
possible volume loss. Hypoxia may be present because of atelectasis and reduced
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:00 AM
AAOS | Venous Thromboembolic Disease
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000654
13/22

respiratory drive from anesthetic agents and narcotic agents; however, a high index of
suspicion is warranted and should lead to additional evaluation.
Pulmonary embolism in particular may be challenging to diagnose, and symptoms of
dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain are rare. More subtle findings include cough,
palpitations, apprehension and anxiety, a general feeling of being unwell, and confusion.
Signs most commonly associated with the development of pulmonary embolism include
tachypnea, tachycardia, and fever.
Initial Patient Evaluation

Initial Patient Evaluation
A chest radiograph is obtained to rule out alternative causes of hypoxia, such as
pneumonia, congestive heart failure, and atelectasis. Electrocardiography is performed
to rule out cardiac pathology; tachycardia is the most common electrocardiographic
finding in patients with pulmonary embolism; however, a right ventricular strain pattern
can be observed. Lastly, an arterial blood gas measurement on room air may be useful
for assessing causes of hypoxia. A normal pulse oximetry measurement is not an
alternative to blood gas measurements because patients can hyperventilate to maintain
adequate oxygenation.
Most patients are hypoxic (PaO2 level <80 mm Hg) and hypocapnic (PaCO2 level <35 mm
Hg) and have a high pulmonary alveolar-arterial oxygen gradient (>20 mm Hg). The
pulmonary alveolar-arterial oxygen gradient (indicative of poor gas exchange between
the alveolus and arterial blood supply) can be calculated as (150 − 1.25 [PaCO2]) −
PaO2.26
Ventilation/Perfusion (V/Q) Scanning
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:00 AM
AAOS | Venous Thromboembolic Disease
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000654
14/22

V/Q scans have largely been replaced by CT angiography but were considered the standard of
care for diagnosing pulmonary embolism in the past.
Scans identify mismatch defects, which are areas that are ventilated without associated
perfusion.
The study is assessed or graded as normal, low, intermediate, or high probability based on
criteria determined from prior studies that compared V/Q scans and pulmonary angiograms.
Patients with normal or low-probability scans should be evaluated for alternative sources of
hypoxemia (particularly if evaluation for lower extremity DVT is negative).
Patients with high-probability scans require treatment.
If the scan is intermediate and clinical suspicion is high, the lower extremities should be
assessed for DVT; if negative, high-resolution chest CT or pulmonary angiography is indicated
to rule out pulmonary embolism27
This may be clinically useful if a patient cannot receive contrast because of kidney failure or
allergies.
Because of its lower volume of irradiation, it also may be useful for follow-up studies after
treatment, in patients with chronic VTE and pulmonary embolism, and during pregnancy.
High-Resolution (Helical or Spiral) Chest CT Angiography
Widely adopted as the first-line imaging modality for diagnosing pulmonary embolism given
the high rate of indeterminate V/Q scans and the accuracy of this technique compared with
other imaging modalities
CT angiography is associated with a sensitivity of 83% and a specificity of 96%.28
It can be performed faster than a V/Q scan, generally is available at all hours of the day, and
may aid in making alternative diagnoses.
The high level of sensitivity may lead to the detection of smaller, less clinically relevant emboli,
leading to over-management.
Irradiation doses, especially fetal irradiation in pregnant women, has been a concern, and
historically has been greater compared with V/Q scans; however, modern protocols are
narrowing that gap.
Pulmonary Angiography
This is an invasive technique that has little utility in the clinical setting for diagnostic purposes.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:00 AM
AAOS | Venous Thromboembolic Disease
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000654
15/22

Duplex Ultrasonography
Duplex ultrasonography or venous ultrasonography is a clinically useful, noninvasive, and
inexpensive technique for diagnosing venous clots.
It is especially useful in identifying proximal clots but has limitations in small calf veins and
cannot visualize the iliac system in the pelvis.29
The routine postoperative screening of patients via venous ultrasonography has not been
shown to be cost effective.
Lower Extremity Contrast Venography
This is an invasive technique that has little utility in the clinical setting for diagnostic purposes.
D-dimer Level
A d-dimer is a breakdown product of the fibrin component of a clot, and its level can be
measured in the blood.
Elevated levels of d-dimers are associated with pulmonary embolism; however, as an
additional marker of inflammation, its levels also may be elevated postoperatively.
This makes d-dimer level challenging to use in postoperative patients; however, various
studies have shown correlation in various postoperative populations.
It is most clinically useful for ruling out pulmonary embolism if its value is low and the clinical
pretest probability also is low.30
Management
CHEST Guidelines for Management of VTE

CHEST Guidelines for Management of VTE
Dosages for agents used to manage DVT and pulmonary embolism are higher than
prophylactic dosages.
For VTE in patients with no cancer history, dabigatran, rivaroxaban, apixaban, or
edoxaban are recommended over vitamin K antagonist (coumadin). Vitamin K
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:00 AM
AAOS | Venous Thromboembolic Disease
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000654
16/22

antagonists are preferable to LMWH. For VTE in patients with a cancer diagnosis, LMWH
is recommended over other agents.
In patients with a subsegmental pulmonary embolus and no evidence of DVT who have a
low risk of VTE recurrence, guidelines suggest surveillance rather than anticoagulation.
In patients at high risk for recurrence, anticoagulation is recommended. In patients who
can be treated via anticoagulation, IVC filters are not recommended.
In patients with DVT and pulmonary embolism provoked by surgical treatment, 3 months
of treatment is recommended.31
IVC Filters

IVC Filters
IVC filters are retrievable devices that typically are placed preoperatively. Because of the
potential complications, including DVT distal to the device, migration, and perforation,
they should be retrieved as soon as anticoagulation can be restarted or the risk of
pulmonary embolism no longer warrants their continued use. Low rates of subsequent
retrieval have been reported because of numerous factors, and all patients with an IVC
filter should be considered for retrieval. This may fall on the treating orthopaedic
surgeon to help coordinate.32
The absolute indication for the use of an IVC filter is if a patient requires anticoagulation
for a DVT or pulmonary embolism but has a contraindication to anticoagulation.
Although expanded indications for IVC filter placement include recurrent VTE,
progression of DVT, massive or high-risk pulmonary embolism with concurrent DVT, and
thrombolysis of an iliocaval DVT, societal recommendations differ widely.31 Prophylactic
use is more controversial but may be considered in consultation with a hematologist if
patients are deemed to be high risk based on their history or the presence of a
hypercoagulable disease.

In a randomized controlled trial, 400 patients were randomly assigned to an IVC filter or
no IVC filter; patients were then further randomized to receive UFH versus LMWH.
Although the IVC filter group had lower rates of pulmonary embolism compared with the
no IVC filter group (1.1% versus 4.8%), a higher rate of subsequent DVT was observed in
the IVC filter group compared with the no IVC filter group (20.8% versus 11.6%) and no
difference was observed in mortality.33 A more recent study evaluated 240 severely
injured trauma patients who had a contraindication to anticoagulant agents and
randomized them to an IVC filter or no IVC filter. At 90 days, no difference in the
incidence of symptomatic pulmonary embolism or death was noted between the two
groups.34
DVT Below the Knee/Calf Veins

DVT Below the Knee/Calf Veins
Based on CHEST guidelines, DVT below the knee/calf veins do not require management
unless symptoms are severe. However, proximal extension can occur in 10% to 20% of
patients, and repeat ultrasonography should be performed to evaluate for propagation 2
weeks later.
Anticoagulant treatment is withheld unless proximal extension is identified.31
Clinical practice is variable, and one study reported that as many as 90% of patients with
below-knee DVT were treated after initial diagnosis.35
